question: A foreign conglomerate offers to build a mega-factory in your poorest district — if it gets a 20-year tax holiday.

option_a.text: Sign it. Jobs today are worth revenue tomorrow.

option_b.text: Refuse. No one gets a free ride on public land.

question: Your city's last public hospital is bankrupt. A private chain offers to take it over and keep it open.

option_a.text: Privatize it. Better run for profit than shut for principle.

option_b.text: Raise taxes and keep it public. Some things aren't for sale.

question: A drought is crushing your farmers. The treasury can fund loan waivers now, or a canal that pays off in ten years.

option_a.text: Build the canal. Real relief beats a good headline.

option_b.text: Waive the loans. People are drowning today, not in ten years.

question: Your biggest donor's factory just failed a pollution audit. The report lands on your desk before the press sees it.

option_a.text: Bury it until after the election. Loyalty has a price.

option_b.text: Release it and personally lead the shutdown.

question: Slum dwellers have occupied land your government already promised to a tech park's investors.

option_a.text: Evict them. A signed deal is a signed deal.

option_b.text: Rehouse every family first, even if the investors walk.

question: The national airline is bleeding money. The unions promise a general strike the day you try to sell it.

option_a.text: Sell it anyway. Taxpayers are not a piggy bank.

option_b.text: Keep it public and absorb the losses. Jobs are policy too.

question: Scientists confirm the new dam will power four million homes — and drown forty villages.

option_a.text: Build it. The greatest good for the greatest number.

option_b.text: Halt it until every displaced family consents to resettlement.

question: Your education minister wants to double teacher salaries — by cutting the highway budget in half.

option_a.text: Refuse. Roads move goods, and goods pay salaries.

option_b.text: Do it. Teachers are building the next fifty years.

question: A crypto exchange will make your city its global headquarters — if you exempt it from banking regulations.

option_a.text: Exempt them. Be the future's first mover.

option_b.text: No exemptions. The rules exist because 2008 happened.

question: A port strike is choking exports. The union's only demand: reinstate two hundred fired workers.

option_a.text: Hire replacements. Nobody holds the economy hostage.

option_b.text: Reinstate them. Labor built this port before capital found it.

question: Your state's groundwater is vanishing. A cola giant's bottling plant is the district's biggest employer — and its biggest well.

option_a.text: Renew the license. A thousand families eat from that plant.

option_b.text: Shut the wells. Water belongs to the village, not the bottle.

question: Insurers want to price premiums using citizens' fitness-tracker data. It would cut costs for the healthy.

option_a.text: Allow it. People who jog shouldn't subsidize people who won't.

option_b.text: Ban it. Your heartbeat is not a credit score.

question: Developers want the old city's heritage quarter for luxury towers. The buildings are crumbling anyway.

option_a.text: Sell. Nostalgia doesn't pay for sewage lines.

option_b.text: Protect it and fund restoration with a tourism levy.

question: A pharma company offers to run free clinics in your district — stocked exclusively with its own drugs.

option_a.text: Accept. Free medicine is free medicine.

option_b.text: Decline. A clinic that's also an advertisement is neither.

question: Ride-hailing drivers are striking for employee status. The platforms threaten to leave your state entirely.

option_a.text: Side with the platforms. Flexibility built this industry.

option_b.text: Side with the drivers. An algorithm is still a boss.

question: Your flagship irrigation scheme is 40% over budget. The auditor suggests quietly reclassifying the overrun.

option_a.text: Reclassify it. The scheme works; the paperwork can flex.

option_b.text: Publish the real numbers and fire the contractor.

question: A mining lease in tribal forest land would fund your entire welfare budget for a decade.

option_a.text: Grant the lease. Poverty is the worse pollutant.

option_b.text: Refuse. Some ground is not yours to sell.

question: Payday lenders are circling your state's factory towns. Banning them leaves workers with loan sharks instead.

option_a.text: License and tax them. Regulated greed beats hidden greed.

option_b.text: Ban them and launch a public credit union.

question: Your power grid needs a bailout. One option: sell citizens' smart-meter usage data to advertisers.

option_a.text: Sell the data. It's anonymous, and the lights stay on.

option_b.text: Raise tariffs on the rich instead. Privacy isn't a fuel.

question: A hedge fund wants to buy your state's grain reserves 'for efficiency'. The offer is embarrassingly generous.

option_a.text: Sell. Warehouses full of rotting grain help no one.

option_b.text: Never. Food security is not a trading position.

question: The city's street vendors are unlicensed, untaxed — and feeding half your workforce lunch for pocket change.

option_a.text: License and tax them. Everyone pays their share.

option_b.text: Leave them be and give them clean water hookups.

question: An automaker will build its plant in your state — if you waive the environmental impact hearing.

option_a.text: Waive it. The hearing is theatre; the jobs are real.

option_b.text: Hold the hearing. Shortcuts poison rivers later.

question: Your pension fund can double returns by investing in a defence manufacturer with a grim export record.

option_a.text: Invest. Pensioners eat returns, not principles.

option_b.text: Divest. Grandmothers shouldn't retire on artillery.

question: A billionaire offers to rebuild every school in your district — with his name on each gate and his foundation writing the syllabus.

option_a.text: Take the deal. Children can't read a principled refusal.

option_b.text: Take the buildings, refuse the syllabus — or nothing.

question: Flood insurance payouts would bankrupt the state fund. Actuaries advise quietly redrawing the flood-risk map.

option_a.text: Redraw it. Solvency now, apologies later.

option_b.text: Publish the honest map and beg the centre for relief.

question: Protesters have blocked the capital's main highway for a week over farm prices.

option_a.text: Clear the road by force. Order must hold.

option_b.text: Walk out and negotiate with them, cameras rolling.

question: Your intelligence chief proposes tapping opposition leaders' phones 'for national security'.

option_a.text: Authorize it. Know your enemies before they know you.

option_b.text: Refuse — and leak the proposal to showcase your clean hands.

question: A rival's supporters heckled your youth wing. Your cadre wants permission to 'respond appropriately'.

option_a.text: Let them. Fear is a currency too.

option_b.text: Forbid it — and stage a silent march past the rival's office.

question: A late-night comedy show mocks you relentlessly. The ratings are enormous.

option_a.text: Have regulators take a sudden interest in the channel's licenses.

option_b.text: Go on the show and roast yourself harder than they ever could.

question: Riots erupt after a religious procession is stoned. Both communities blame each other, and the city is burning.

option_a.text: Curfew and mass arrests tonight. Sort the guilt out later.

option_b.text: Walk unarmed through both neighbourhoods with every camera in the city.

question: A journalist has documents proving your coalition partner ran a land scam.

option_a.text: Pressure her editor. The coalition survives; the story doesn't.

option_b.text: Break the coalition yourself and take credit for the cleanup.

question: An opposition MLA offers to defect — for a ministry and unspecified 'expenses'.

option_a.text: Pay quietly. Numbers are numbers.

option_b.text: Expose the offer at a press conference he doesn't know about.

question: A viral influencer with forty million followers wants to interview you — but only about your personal life.

option_a.text: Decline. The office deserves better than gossip.

option_b.text: Do it. Reach beats gravitas every single time.

question: Your security detail says the death threats are credible. Advisors want you off the campaign trail.

option_a.text: Triple the security cordon and campaign behind glass.

option_b.text: Campaign anyway — in an open jeep, daring them.

question: A general hints, off the record, that the army 'stands with you' if the election result is disputed.

option_a.text: Note it quietly. Insurance is insurance.

option_b.text: Repeat the remark on live TV and watch him deny it.

question: Your party's IT cell has built a deepfake of your rival slurring a minority community. It's flawless.

option_a.text: Release it through cutouts. Deny everything.

option_b.text: Delete it — then announce publicly that you refused to use one.

question: A cricket world cup final falls on election eve. Your rival has bought every ad slot in the broadcast.

option_a.text: Have the broadcast regulator find a problem with the slots.

option_b.text: Show up at the stadium and let the cameras find you.

question: Farmers plan a tractor rally through the capital on Republic Day.

option_a.text: Ban the rally and barricade the highways.

option_b.text: Ride the lead tractor yourself.

question: An anchor who built your image now wants a Rajya Sabha seat. Refuse, and prime time turns hostile.

option_a.text: Refuse — and remind him what your government licenses.

option_b.text: Give him the seat at a gala and make it a spectacle of gratitude.

question: Your own MPs are leaking against you before the leadership vote.

option_a.text: Find the leakers. End their careers quietly, one by one.

option_b.text: Call an open press conference and take every question standing.

question: A foreign documentary crew is filming your district's failures. Their visas are up for renewal on your desk.

option_a.text: Deny the renewal. National image is national interest.

option_b.text: Renew them — and give them a guided tour they'll never forget.

question: The opposition has called a bandh. Shops that open risk their windows; shops that close admit who runs the street.

option_a.text: Deploy police at every market and dare the enforcers to show.

option_b.text: Go shopping yourself, on camera, at the busiest bazaar.

question: A hostile biography drops a week before polls. It's mostly true.

option_a.text: Get an injunction tonight. Argue about truth after the count.

option_b.text: Read the worst chapter aloud at your next rally, laughing.

question: Your convoy gets stuck in a flood-hit village that wasn't on the itinerary. The water is knee-deep and rising.

option_a.text: Push through. Schedules exist because chaos doesn't govern.

option_b.text: Get out, roll up your trousers, and wade in with the rescue teams.

question: A student leader's arrest has made her a national icon. Every day in custody grows her legend.

option_a.text: Keep her in. Letting her walk crowns the defiance.

option_b.text: Release her personally, with flowers, and steal the moment.

question: Exit polls say you've lost. The official count starts in eight hours.

option_a.text: Position loyal observers at every counting centre. Watch everything.

option_b.text: Declare victory tonight anyway and let the count argue with you.

question: Your predecessor's statue is being torn down by a mob that mostly votes for you.

option_a.text: Send the police in hard. Mobs don't get a vote on history.

option_b.text: Arrive with a megaphone and redirect the crowd to a rally.

question: A hacker collective threatens to dump your party's internal chats unless you drop the surveillance bill.

option_a.text: Never negotiate. Trace them and make arrests before the dump.

option_b.text: Dump the chats yourself first, annotated, with commentary.

question: Your national anthem plays before every film screening. A viral video shows a man who didn't stand being beaten.

option_a.text: Defend the beating crowd's 'sentiment' and tighten the rule.

option_b.text: Visit the man in hospital and stand for him, cameras in tow.

question: The census leaked early, and it's bad news for your base's majority in three districts.

option_a.text: Delay official publication indefinitely. Numbers can wait.

option_b.text: Release it with a slick 'New India' campaign that reframes everything.

question: A border skirmish leaves three soldiers dead. Elections are in two months.

option_a.text: Order a televised retaliatory strike.

option_b.text: Quietly settle it and redirect the defence surge into ports and roads.

question: The census shows your rival's community is now the majority in a district you hold.

option_a.text: Redraw the boundaries before the next poll.

option_b.text: Buy their loyalty with a targeted welfare package.

question: Illegal gold mines employ ten thousand people in your hills — and fund the local strongman who delivers you votes.

option_a.text: Leave them alone. The strongman's machine is your machine.

option_b.text: Legalize, license, and tax every shaft.

question: Your police want military-grade drones for 'crowd management'. The manufacturer is offering a bulk discount.

option_a.text: Buy the fleet. Visible power prevents its use.

option_b.text: Skip the drones; lease them the hardware only when courts approve.

question: A separatist region offers peace — if you grant it control of its own mineral royalties.

option_a.text: Refuse. The map is not a negotiation.

option_b.text: Take the deal. Peace is cheaper than garrisons.

question: Smugglers run the border economy. Every crackdown collapses the bazaar towns that depend on them.

option_a.text: Crack down anyway. A porous border is a broken state.

option_b.text: Open a free-trade zone and turn smugglers into taxpayers.

question: Your army chief wants conscription revived. Industry says it would gut their young workforce.

option_a.text: Revive it. A nation that won't serve won't survive.

option_b.text: Refuse and fund a volunteer force with corporate partnership.

question: A tycoon under fraud investigation is your largest single employer. His arrest would crater three townships.

option_a.text: Arrest him at dawn, on camera. No one is above the state.

option_b.text: Negotiate a settlement: he pays back double and keeps the plants running.

question: Foreign social apps refuse to open local data centres. Your security agencies want them banned.

option_a.text: Ban them. Sovereignty over servers.

option_b.text: Threaten the ban, then sell them compliance at a price.

question: Your home minister wants a registry of every citizen's biometrics. A consortium offers to build it for free — keeping a copy.

option_a.text: Build it in-house, whatever it costs. The state shares nothing.

option_b.text: Take the free build. Data is cheaper to share than to gather.

question: Gangs run the transport unions. A national logistics firm will invest — if you break them first.

option_a.text: Break them with midnight raids and televised perp walks.

option_b.text: Let the firm buy the gangs out. Money launders faster than blood.

question: A sanctions list lands on your desk. Complying costs your exporters billions; defying costs you an ally.

option_a.text: Defy it loudly. Great nations don't take dictation.

option_b.text: Comply publicly, and quietly route trade through a third flag.

question: Your state lottery funds hospitals — and bankrupts the poorest wards that play it most.

option_a.text: Ban it. Vice is not a revenue model.

option_b.text: Double the jackpot and earmark every rupee for the same wards.

question: An arms fair wants to book your capital's convention centre. Activists promise a siege.

option_a.text: Host it under heavy guard. Strength attracts strength.

option_b.text: Host it, triple the venue fee, and tax every deal signed inside.

question: Fuel subsidies are bankrupting the treasury, but removing them sparked riots the last time anyone tried.

option_a.text: Remove them overnight, with troops pre-positioned.

option_b.text: Phase them out behind a cash-transfer scheme people can see.

question: Your intelligence bureau catches a rival party taking foreign money. Exposing it means revealing you were spying on them.

option_a.text: Expose it. The treason headline buries the spying one.

option_b.text: Blackmail them privately into backing your finance bill.

question: A doomsday cult has bought an entire village and pays quadruple the local wage.

option_a.text: Raid the compound before it becomes a headline.

option_b.text: Tax them like any employer and audit them into the open.

question: Your currency is in free fall. The central bank governor refuses to burn reserves defending it.

option_a.text: Replace him tonight with someone who follows orders.

option_b.text: Back him publicly and let the currency find its floor.

question: Militants freed your kidnapped engineers after a 'facilitation fee' was paid by the contractor. The press is asking.

option_a.text: Deny everything and bomb the militants' camp for the record.

option_b.text: Call it the cost of doing business and re-tender with better insurance.

question: Your navy seized a trawler full of contraband — registered to a shell company two donations away from your party.

option_a.text: Prosecute everyone and let the chips fall.

option_b.text: Auction the cargo, fine the shell, and lose the paperwork.

question: A city ward is a no-go zone run by a 'community council' that keeps the peace better than your police ever did.

option_a.text: Retake the ward. There is one law and it wears your uniform.

option_b.text: Contract them officially as a neighbourhood service provider.

question: The rail unions demand a safety overhaul after a derailment. The overhaul halts freight for six months.

option_a.text: Order the trains to keep running under a new 'emergency protocol'.

option_b.text: Halt freight, compensate industry, and bill the repairs as stimulus.

question: Pirated textbooks sell at a tenth of the price. Publishers demand raids; parents pray you look away.

option_a.text: Raid the printers. Property is property.

option_b.text: Bulk-license the books and sell them legally at the pirate price.

question: A retired general is building a private security empire staffed by his old battalion. He's loyal — for now.

option_a.text: Absorb his firm into the state apparatus before it outgrows you.

option_b.text: Give him government contracts and make his fortune depend on yours.

question: Your prisons are at triple capacity. A conglomerate offers to build and run new ones, paid per prisoner.

option_a.text: Keep prisons in state hands and expand them with the defence budget.

option_b.text: Sign the contract. The per-head rate is genuinely excellent.

question: A viral video shows your party worker bribing a booth official. The press wants a statement within the hour.

option_a.text: Call it a deepfake and flood the cycle with counter-stories.

option_b.text: Expel the worker publicly and demand an independent inquiry.

question: A celebrity offers to headline your rally — for a seat in the upper house.

option_a.text: Deal. Star power wins elections; purity doesn't.

option_b.text: Refuse. Seats are earned, not gifted at after-parties.

question: Two hours before your flagship rally, the venue's roof is declared unsafe.

option_a.text: Move it to the streets — bigger crowd, better optics.

option_b.text: Cancel it and refund every attendee's travel.

question: Your ghostwriter's memoir manuscript paints you as a saint. Chapter six never happened.

option_a.text: Publish. Legends are built, not fact-checked.

option_b.text: Cut the chapter and publish the flawed, true version.

question: A grieving mother from the stampede at your rally goes viral asking to meet you.

option_a.text: Meet her at a televised event with a compensation cheque.

option_b.text: Meet her privately, no cameras, and fund the inquiry she asks for.

question: Your data team can micro-target anxious first-time voters with tailored fear ads. It polls brilliantly.

option_a.text: Run the ads. Fear clicks; hope scrolls past.

option_b.text: Refuse, and pledge publicly to publish every ad you run.

question: A film about your life is in production. The director wants final cut; your team wants approval rights.

option_a.text: Demand approval. Your story, your edit.

option_b.text: Give the director final cut and take your chances with the truth.

question: Your child's wedding could be a quiet family affair — or a three-day spectacle with every ally and donor in attendance.

option_a.text: The spectacle. Weddings are summits with better food.

option_b.text: Keep it private and donate the difference, receipts public.

question: A rival collapses mid-debate, on stage, on camera. The moderator looks at you.

option_a.text: Rush to his side and hold the frame until the ambulance comes.

option_b.text: Clear the hall, suspend the debate, and say nothing to the press.

question: Pollsters say voters can't name a single policy of yours — but they know your slogan, your dog, and your lucky shawl.

option_a.text: Lean in. The shawl gets its own merchandise line.

option_b.text: Scrap the branding budget and hold town halls on policy only.

question: Your team leaked a fake 'internal memo' to bait the opposition into a false attack. It's working beautifully.

option_a.text: Let it run. Their credibility burns; your hands look clean.

option_b.text: Kill the operation and own up before it detonates.

question: A temple, a church, and a mosque all invite you for the same festival evening. Attending one offends two.

option_a.text: Attend all three with a camera crew and call it a pilgrimage.

option_b.text: Attend none, and host an open interfaith dinner at your residence.

question: An orphaned boy you posed with in a flood-relief photo is now homeless again. A reporter found him.

option_a.text: Re-stage the reunion — bigger, better, with a house key this time.

option_b.text: House him quietly and fix the scheme that failed him.

question: Your speechwriter quit and published every draft you rejected — including the honest ones.

option_a.text: Deliver the most brutal rejected draft at your next rally, verbatim.

option_b.text: Thank her publicly and admit which drafts you wish you'd given.

question: A stray dog adopted your campaign office and the internet has fallen in love with it.

option_a.text: Make it the campaign mascot. Merch by Friday.

option_b.text: Use the moment to fund the city's first real animal shelter.

question: Your opponent's teenage daughter is being savaged online by accounts your IT cell 'doesn't control'.

option_a.text: Condemn the trolling in a soft-focus video that trends for days.

option_b.text: Shut the accounts down and hand the server logs to her family's lawyers.

question: A quiz show invites you on for charity. Your staff can get the questions in advance.

option_a.text: Take the questions. Winning is the story.

option_b.text: Go in cold and lose with grace if you must.

question: Monsoon floods hit on polling week. Relief trucks can carry your party stickers, or they can leave now.

option_a.text: Sticker every truck. Aid unclaimed is aid wasted.

option_b.text: Send them unmarked tonight.

question: Your old debate clips are being remixed into flattering AI mashups by fans. They're not accurate, but they're glorious.

option_a.text: Amplify them. Myth travels lighter than transcript.

option_b.text: Post corrections under each one, even the flattering ones.

question: The stadium you promised is half-built and the money's gone. The inauguration is already scheduled.

option_a.text: Inaugurate the finished half at night, lit like a dream.

option_b.text: Cancel the event and publish the forensic audit instead.

question: A dying organizer's last wish is a debate with you. Your advisors call it a trap with a halo.

option_a.text: Accept — and produce it as the television event of the year.

option_b.text: Visit him off-camera and answer every question he has, alone.

question: Your approval is cratering. A consultant proposes a 'manufactured comeback': staged setback, staged redemption.

option_a.text: Run the arc. Voters love a resurrection.

option_b.text: Fire the consultant and let the numbers say what they say.

question: A schoolgirl's question — 'Why did you lie about the lake cleanup?' — is trending from your town hall.

option_a.text: Invite her to co-host your next broadcast about the lake.

option_b.text: Answer her in writing, publish the letter, and restart the cleanup.

question: Your party anthem was plagiarized from a folk singer who died poor. Her granddaughter just found out.

option_a.text: Sign the granddaughter as the anthem's official voice, royalties attached.

option_b.text: Pay the estate back-royalties and credit the singer at every rally.

question: A billionaire offers to fund your entire campaign — anonymously, through shell trusts.

option_a.text: Decline theatrically and launch a televised crowdfunding marathon.

option_b.text: Decline quietly and cap every donation at a worker's day-wage.

question: Your state's film industry demands subsidies after streaming gutted theatre revenue.

option_a.text: Let the market decide what people watch.

option_b.text: Subsidize it — and premiere every funded film at your rallies.

question: The IPL wants your city as a franchise host. The stadium bid would eat the metro extension's budget.

option_a.text: Fund the metro. Commuters vote; spectators cheer.

option_b.text: Win the franchise and throw the opening ceremony of the decade.

question: A statue of your party's icon is proposed — taller than any in the world, at the cost of a small city's budget.

option_a.text: Scale it down and put the difference into industrial parks.

option_b.text: Build it taller. Skylines are arguments you win forever.

question: Your tourism board can market the state's beaches — or its slums, where a hit film was shot.

option_a.text: Beaches. Sell what people pay to see twice.

option_b.text: The slum tour, narrated by the film's star. Controversy is currency.

question: A unicorn founder wants to livestream a cabinet meeting 'for transparency'. His platform gets the exclusive.

option_a.text: Refuse the stream, but sell the platform your press briefings instead.

option_b.text: Stream it. Government as content; you as the lead.

question: The budget speech is tomorrow. Your advisors drafted an honest, boring one; your instincts want fireworks.

option_a.text: Boring and credible. Markets punish poetry.

option_b.text: Fireworks. Announce the moonshot; fund it later.

question: An airline will paint your face on a plane for the inaugural route to your constituency.

option_a.text: Decline the paint job; negotiate cheaper cargo rates instead.

option_b.text: Take the livery and fly the first flight yourself, waving.

question: A gaming company offers your likeness for their election-strategy game. Royalty per download.

option_a.text: Negotiate equity, not royalties, and stay out of the trailer.

option_b.text: Voice the character yourself and stream the launch.

question: Your ministry can announce the jobs data quietly on Friday evening — or you can own the bad numbers at a press meet.

option_a.text: Friday evening. Markets read footnotes; voters don't.

option_b.text: Own it live, with a whiteboard, and pin the blame where it sells.

question: A luxury brand wants to sponsor the republic's anniversary parade.

option_a.text: Take the sponsorship and cut the parade from the budget entirely.

option_b.text: Refuse the logo but borrow their creative director for the show.

question: Your state fair is a money pit, but four million people come every year and every one of them sees your face.

option_a.text: Privatize the fair and take a cut of the gate.

option_b.text: Double the budget and headline the closing night yourself.

question: An OTT platform wants to make a docuseries on your government — full access, no veto.

option_a.text: Charge them for access and cap the filming days.

option_b.text: Full access. You'll simply out-perform the edit.

question: The old textile mill could be auctioned to developers — or become the venue for the biggest music festival in the country.

option_a.text: Auction it. Land appreciates; festivals evaporate.

option_b.text: Festival. A hundred thousand kids screaming in your city, annually.

question: Your face recognition pilot caught a famous fugitive at a wedding. Announce the tech, and the courts descend.

option_a.text: Stay quiet, credit 'police work', and quietly renew the contract.

option_b.text: Announce it with the arrest footage. Let the courts chase the applause.

question: A rival state poached your auto plant with tax breaks. Your team drafted two responses: a counter-offer, or a very funny billboard.

option_a.text: The counter-offer. Factories outlast punchlines.

option_b.text: The billboard. Make the poachers a national joke.

question: Space agency scientists want funding for a modest climate satellite. Your advisors want a flag on the moon.

option_a.text: The satellite. It pays for itself in crop forecasts.

option_b.text: The moon. Nobody ever wept at a crop forecast.

question: Your city's iconic bridge needs repairs. Engineers want it closed for a year; event planners want a farewell festival on it first.

option_a.text: Close it tonight. Liability is not a photo op.

option_b.text: One last festival — fireworks, then scaffolding.

question: A tycoon's daughter's wedding wants to book the heritage fort for a week, closing it to the public.

option_a.text: Rent it at an eye-watering rate, earmarked for restoration.

option_b.text: Refuse — then host a free public concert at the fort that weekend.

question: Your new expressway needs a name. The bankers financing it suggested theirs.

option_a.text: Sell the naming rights. Concrete doesn't care what it's called.

option_b.text: Name it after a beloved poet and recite her at the ribbon.

question: A meme account with ten million followers will endorse you — if you follow back and reply to one meme a week.

option_a.text: Buy the account outright through an agency instead.

option_b.text: Reply to the memes personally. Become the meme.

question: Your health ministry's anti-smoking campaign is ready. The tobacco lobby offers to fund double the airtime — with softer wording.

option_a.text: Take their money and their wording. Reach is reach.

option_b.text: Run the brutal version and cast a dying film star who volunteered.

question: An airline strands two hundred pilgrims at midnight. Your office can book them buses — or you can arrive at the airport at 2 a.m.

option_a.text: Book the buses, invoice the airline, and fine them at dawn.

option_b.text: Arrive at 2 a.m. with chai and camera crews.

question: The national broadcaster wants to auction your weekly radio slot to private bidders.

option_a.text: Let them auction it — and take a revenue share for the exchequer.

option_b.text: Keep the slot and turn it into a live phone-in with no screening.

question: A start-up will drone-deliver medicine to your hill villages. Their demo crashed last month, spectacularly.

option_a.text: Pilot it quietly in two villages with insurance in writing.

option_b.text: Launch it live on television, first package to a war widow.

question: Your budget has one crore left: a small-business credit line, or floodlights for the night cricket league every ward plays in.

option_a.text: The credit line. Compounding beats cheering.

option_b.text: The floodlights — and bowl the first over yourself.

question: A militant fringe group publicly endorses you. Disowning them may cost you a swing district.

option_a.text: Stay silent. Votes don't ask for character certificates.

option_b.text: Reject the endorsement on live television.

question: A informant in your own ministry alleges inflated defence contracts.

option_a.text: Transfer him somewhere quiet and audit internally.

option_b.text: Protect him publicly and open the books.

question: Election eve: a rumor spreads that voting machines in your stronghold are rigged — in your favor.

option_a.text: Dismiss it and accuse rivals of sore-loser tactics.

option_b.text: Demand a full recount yourself before anyone else asks.

question: A textbook committee wants to rewrite history chapters your base finds 'insulting'.

option_a.text: Approve the rewrite. Pride builds nations.

option_b.text: Block it. History is not a campaign asset.

question: Your party's founder — long dead — is accused in a new memoir of rigging his first election.

option_a.text: Sue the publisher and rally the faithful at his memorial.

option_b.text: Commission an open historical inquiry, whatever it finds.

question: Police shot a gangster in a 'staged encounter'. Half the city is celebrating; the other half knows what staged means.

option_a.text: Decorate the officers. Some verdicts can't wait for courts.

option_b.text: Order a judicial probe into the encounter, celebrations be damned.

question: An anti-conversion bill would thrill your base and terrify a minority that has never voted for you anyway.

option_a.text: Pass it. Govern for the people who show up for you.

option_b.text: Kill it in committee and absorb the base's anger.

question: Your nephew was caught on tape threatening a contractor 'in your name'.

option_a.text: Bury the tape and remind the contractor whose district this is.

option_b.text: Hand the tape to the police and your nephew to a lawyer.

question: A curfew-breaking funeral procession for a beloved cleric is heading to the old city. Ten thousand mourners, zero permits.

option_a.text: Stop it at the gates. A curfew that bends is not a curfew.

option_b.text: Lift the curfew for the night and walk with the mourners.

question: The sedition law is a colonial relic — and the sharpest knife in your drawer.

option_a.text: Keep it. You didn't write the law; you just inherited its uses.

option_b.text: Repeal it while you're strong enough to survive without it.

question: Your challenger was jailed on old charges the courts suddenly remembered. Everyone assumes it was you. It wasn't.

option_a.text: Say nothing. Useful assumptions are still useful.

option_b.text: Demand her bail publicly and beat her fair in the open.

question: A frontier village keeps voting for the separatists. The army suggests relocating it 'for its own safety'.

option_a.text: Relocate it. Geography is loyalty.

option_b.text: Build the school and clinic they've asked about for thirty years.

question: An informer inside a protest camp has been feeding you everything. He's just been discovered, and the camp is deciding his fate.

option_a.text: Extract him with force tonight, whatever the footage looks like.

option_b.text: Confess the operation, disband it, and negotiate his safe release.

question: Your interior ministry drafted a list of NGOs to be 'financially reviewed'. Every name on it once criticized you.

option_a.text: Sign it. Coincidences happen to critics.

option_b.text: Shred it and order reviews by random lottery instead.

question: A lynch mob's ringleader turns out to be your booth committee president in a village you can't win without.

option_a.text: Let the case crawl. The village will forget; the booth won't.

option_b.text: Expel him today and testify if they call you.

question: The blasphemy case against a poet is legally hollow, but dropping it means facing the mob that filed it.

option_a.text: Let the case run for years. Process is its own punishment.

option_b.text: Withdraw it and read her poem from your office steps.

question: Your bodyguards beat a man who lunged at you. He turns out to have been reaching for a petition.

option_a.text: Stand by your detail. Hesitation gets leaders killed.

option_b.text: Visit him in hospital, read the petition, and act on it.

question: An election in a neighbouring country was stolen in broad daylight. Their opposition asks for your voice; their junta controls your gas pipeline.

option_a.text: Congratulate the junta. Warm homes over warm feelings.

option_b.text: Call the theft a theft and start pricing alternative gas.

question: Your prisons chief proposes solitary confinement for the hunger-striking political prisoners 'to protect them'.

option_a.text: Approve it. Martyrdom needs an audience; remove the audience.

option_b.text: Meet the strikers yourself and hear the demands first-hand.

question: A convicted don is winning his prison-cell election campaign in your alliance's ticket.

option_a.text: Keep him on the ticket. His ward delivers, cell or no cell.

option_b.text: Tear up the alliance seat and run a schoolteacher instead.

question: The riot commission's report is finished. It names two of your ministers.

option_a.text: Classify it 'pending review' until after the election.

option_b.text: Table it in full and sack both ministers by evening.

question: Refugees from a border war are camping at your state's edge. Winter arrives in six weeks.

option_a.text: Seal the border. Sympathy doesn't scale.

option_b.text: Open the schools as shelters and register every child.

question: A code word in your party's chat groups triggers coordinated harassment of any journalist who crosses you. You just learned it exists.

option_a.text: Leave it running. You never ordered it; you merely benefit.

option_b.text: Expose and dismantle it, naming the coordinators.

question: Your old mentor, now senile, keeps making communal remarks at party events. The base loves him.

option_a.text: Keep him on stage. He says what you can't.

option_b.text: Retire him with honour and a public thank-you tour.

question: The opposition offers a pact: neither side runs candidates with criminal records. Their list is longer than yours — barely.

option_a.text: Refuse. Never let rivals write your candidate list.

option_b.text: Sign it on stage, shaking hands, and dare them to honor it.
